vignette:
Mere's life changed on an overcast winter afternoon when, at 65, she was driving home alone after work from her cybersecurity office in Auckland's edge-of-business district, the car skidding on a wet stretch of road and striking a barrier hard enough to leave her pinned for what felt like hours. She survived, but the crash was violent and disorienting, and what stayed with her most was not just the impact itself but the helplessness of being trapped inside it, hearing metal grind and tasting blood while waiting for help. In the weeks after, Mere found that the memory did not arrive as a clear story so much as a series of images: the angle of the dashboard, the blur of rain on the windshield, the flash of the barrier, a body jolted sideways. Each time that memory broke through, it seemed to confirm the thought that followed it: if this could return so vividly and with such force, then something must be deeply wrong with her, and maybe that damage was now part of who she was. At times, just thinking about it brought back the smell of hot rubber and petrol, and with it a sharp ache in the same parts of her body that had been injured in the collision. She had come to believe that her own body could not be trusted anymore, that it had failed her at the very moment she needed it, and she felt the whole thing was deeply unfair - a senseless accident that had never been properly answered for. Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, Mere moved through ordinary settings as if danger were already there; the threat did not wait for anything new to happen, because her belief that she could not protect herself made every unfamiliar road and every quiet room feel like a test she was already failing. What unsettled her almost as much was the sense that others could see the event written on her, that people at work might look at her and somehow know what had happened. That constant sense of danger quietly hardened into a conviction that she was marked and exposed, and it was that feeling of threat that made the accident seem like proof of a lasting flaw rather than a passing misfortune.

Those beliefs quickly shaped the way Mere tried to live. She found herself going over and over why the crash had happened to her, asking herself whether she had missed some warning on the road or whether there was something wrong with her now that made disaster more likely. Because the event felt so unjust and because she no longer trusted her own body, she began to keep herself from anything that might stir feeling of any kind: she shut down conversations with her late husband's friends, avoided looking at the damaged car photos, and even turned away from music and television shows that might make her feel too much. She had been pushing the whole thing away for so long that the effort of not thinking about it kept the memory alive and close; each attempt to shut it down seemed to leave it returning later in sharper, more intrusive fragments, which only made her more convinced that she was unsafe in her own mind. She also tried, as she put it, to erase the memory altogether, forcing herself not to dwell on the crash and pushing away reminders whenever they appeared. Yet the more she fought the images, the more they intruded in fragments. When her mind went back to the accident, the pictures returned with unusual force, and with them the smell, the bodily pain, and the certainty that the event had marked her in some visible way. That made her even more convinced that she was exposed to others and could be read at a glance, which only deepened her efforts to shut down thought and feeling.

The aftermath became a tightening pattern around sleep. Mere found it hard to fall asleep unless she stayed alert, as if closing her eyes meant lowering her guard in a world that had already proven unsafe. When the threat felt that close, staying alert and checking her surroundings was the only thing that seemed sensible to her; she kept watch because, in her mind, lowering it even briefly might let the same kind of harm reach her again. Nighttime felt more dangerous than the day, and in the dark of her house she would wake and check whether she was safe, listening for sounds and scanning the room before allowing herself to settle again. Those nights were not calm, because the images from the crash often returned in the quiet: the picture-like flashes of the barrier, the interior of the car, the body pain that seemed to come back with them. Once she was awake and watching, she was more likely to think that she still could not trust her body and that the accident remained unanswered and unjust. And once those thoughts took hold, she became more determined to suppress them - to avoid feeling, to stop the mind's replay, to push the memory away - but the effort never really worked. Instead, the constant checking and mental strain made it harder to rest, and the deprivation made the images feel sharper, more unavoidable, and more threatening.

Over time, Mere's world narrowed. She still worked as a cybersecurity analyst, but she found herself staying late less often and avoiding the long evening drive home whenever she could, arranging her day around the hours when she felt safer on the road. At home, she kept the lights on longer than before and disliked being left alone in the quiet after dark. Staying in smaller, more controlled spaces and avoiding anything that might stir the memory had kept her nervous system from ever learning that she could be safe again, so the threat still felt real and immediate whenever the house went quiet. The loneliness that followed her widowhood made the nights feel even more exposed, though she rarely said that directly. What eventually brought her to seek help was the sense that her life had become organized around bracing against the accident rather than living beyond it. She was exhausted by the repeated checking, the sleeplessness, and the relentless returning of pictures and smells she could not keep out. What frightened Mere most now was the possibility that this would never lift - that her body would remain unreliable, the injustice unresolved, and the crash something others could somehow still see in her face unless she found a way to stop it from ruling her nights.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows negative beliefs but does not clearly state that they themselves lead to a sense of threat or danger in the same paragraph.
The memory is described as intruding, but the text does not clearly say that the traumatic memory drives Mere’s negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
The vignette shows feeling unsafe and checking behavior, but it does not clearly state that threat directly leads to her maladaptive strategies in the same paragraph.
The sense of threat is present, but the text does not clearly say it causes or intensifies her negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
The vignette describes avoidance and suppression, but it does not clearly state that these maladaptive strategies bring back the memory in the same paragraph.
The vignette shows avoidance and hypervigilance, but it does not clearly state that these strategies increase her sense of threat in the same paragraph.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette shows negative beliefs but does not clearly state that they themselves lead to a sense of threat or danger in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The memory is described as intruding, but the text does not clearly say that the traumatic memory drives Mere’s negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows feeling unsafe and checking behavior, but it does not clearly state that threat directly leads to her maladaptive strategies in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The sense of threat is present, but the text does not clearly say it causes or intensifies her negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette describes avoidance and suppression, but it does not clearly state that these maladaptive strategies bring back the memory in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette shows avoidance and hypervigilance, but it does not clearly state that these strategies increase her sense of threat in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
